newsitem.title: CANADA: CAW says no progress in talks with GM Canada.
newsitem.headline: CAW says no progress in talks with GM Canada.

text.p: Talks aimed at settling a strike against General Motors Corp. in Canada made no progress Thursday, meaning more than 15,000 workers will stay off the job for a second day, the Canadian Auto Workers union said.

"There has been no offer, no change," CAW President Buzz Hargrove said after afternoon talks with GM Canada chief negotiator Dean Munger. "You're looking at day two for sure. It couldn't possibly happen today."
Hargrove said he talked to Munger three times Thursday afternoon and that local and subcommittee bargaining had taken place, but there was no real progress on any issue.
GM Canada spokesman Stew Low said earlier Thursday it was too early to expect the company to make a new offer. "There's still a lot of talking to do to try to get things back on track," said Low.

Some 15,500 workers at GM Canada's Oshawa, Ontario, and Ste-Therese, Quebec, assembly plants went on strike late on Wednesday after the company presented its first full-scale economic offer, which Hargrove called "an insult." The union had set a strike deadline just before midnight on Wednesday.
Under the union's escalating strike strategy, other GM Canada plants were to join the strike on Sunday and all 26,000 union workers could be on strike by Oct. 9 if no deal was reached.

Analysts said that a strike by all GM union workers in Canada could cost the world's largest automaker $100 million to $150 million a week and eventually spill over and start forcing plants to shut down in the United States.

Separate talks continued between GM and the United Auto Workers union in the United States. UAW President Stephen Yokich said the union needs to make strategy decisions of its own and will confer with CAW leaders on how to proceed.
Hargrove said he spoke to Yokich Thursday and was assured the UAW would not make any moves that would steal bargaining power from the Canadian union.
"He reiterated his commitment he's not going to put any strike deadline or do anything to take any power away from our bargaining table," Hargrove said.

While talks resumed in Toronto, Hargrove said the two sides remained "worlds apart" on the major issue of outsourcing -- the use of outside, usually non-union workers -- as well as hours and work rule issues. He said he believes the Canadian talks were sunk by GM's Detroit headquarters.

"I think Detroit has put a halt to the bargaining," Hargrove told reporters after meeting with GM Canada's Munger Thursday. "We're on strike because someone (in Detroit) has failed to recognize that there is another country in this industry."

Hargrove said the strike would last until a contract was reached that mirrored the agreement the CAW and Chrysler Corp. reached on Sept. 17. That pact gave the CAW broad input into future decisions on outsourcing at Chrsyler.
"We'll stay out until the pattern is there," said Hargrove. "We are not leaving this bargaining until we have every word that is in the Chrysler job security language." Munger said
the strike would have a "severe impact" on GM Canada's operations but declined to speculate when the impact would reach U.S. operations or cripple GM's just-in-time parts supply strategy.
GM said earlier that a strike in Canada would not affect talks with the UAW in the United States. "We're working pretty much independently," GM spokesman Gerry Holmes said.

The CAW has said its C$50 million ($36.5 million) strike fund could last up to eight weeks and stretch to 16 weeks if new credit is arranged. The union also has set a special meeting for Oct. 18 to raise funds from all 210,000 members of the CAW.
Workers at GM's St. Catharines, Ontario, engine and components plant were to join the strike on Oct. 6 and all Canadian operations will be shut down by Oct. 9 under the escalating strike plan.
More than 350 union leaders from plants across Ontario and Quebec were to meet on Friday in Toronto to discuss the negotiations and the strike.
Economists said a prolonged strike against GM in Canada could hurt the country's fledgling economic recovery, shaving up to 1 point off growth in the fourth quarter.
"I think a short strike would have only a transitory effect, but a long one could be very damaging," said John McCallum, chief economist at Royal Bank of Canada in Toronto.
